course.title: System Security
course.description: A practitioner-oriented System Security course focused on securing operating systems, servers, services, identities, filesystems, processes, and administrative paths. Students progress from host-security fundamentals through secure baselines, configuration management, least privilege, Linux capabilities, SSH hardening, SELinux, service isolation, patching, software integrity, Windows and Linux endpoint security, logging, file-integrity monitoring, and incident response. The course culminates in a read-only System Security Baseline Auditor that turns hardening requirements into evidence-backed control findings. It is appropriate for learners who know basic computing and are ready to work with Linux and Windows security concepts in authorized lab environments.
prerequisites: Comfort with a command line and navigating files.
Basic understanding of users, processes, networking, and software installation is recommended.
A local Linux VM is strongly recommended for hands-on work; a Windows VM is useful for the endpoint-baseline lesson.
Only assess systems you own or are explicitly authorized to assess.
learningOutcomes: Explain system-security goals, trust boundaries, threats, vulnerabilities, and risk.
Create and assess role-specific security baselines using authoritative configuration guidance.
Reduce host attack surface through service, account, privilege, and management-path controls.
Apply Linux permissions, ACLs, capabilities, SELinux concepts, and service isolation to reduce blast radius.
Design secure SSH administration and privileged-access models.
Build patching, software-integrity, configuration-drift, and control-assessment workflows.
Evaluate Windows and Linux host-hardening controls and security telemetry.
Investigate suspicious host activity using evidence-aware triage and response principles.
Write measurable system-security findings with evidence, risk rationale, remediation, and verification steps.
Build, test, and operate a read-only system-security baseline auditor.

modules.title: System Security Foundations
modules.description: Establish a host-security mental model: assets, trust boundaries, threat surfaces, security properties, and defense-in-depth.

lessons.title: System Security Goals and Trust Boundaries
lessons.description: Explain how system security protects hosts, workloads, identities, data, and management paths.
learningObjectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, accountability, and resilience in host-security contexts.
Identify trust boundaries between users, processes, services, administrators, and external systems.
Connect security goals to concrete system controls.

notes.text: System security is the practice of keeping a computing system trustworthy despite faults, misuse, malicious activity, and changing conditions. A useful model starts by naming what must be protected and what trust assumptions exist.

items: Confidentiality limits unauthorized disclosure.
Integrity protects against unauthorized modification.
Availability concerns timely access to required services.
Trust boundaries are places where identity, privilege, data, or control assumptions change.

notes.text:
Example trust-boundary questions:
- Who can start this service?
- Which identity does it run as?
- Which files can it write?
- Which network peers can reach it?
A secure boundary is enforced by controls; simply drawing a boundary does not create security.

quiz.question: Which property is primarily affected when an attacker changes a system configuration without authorization?
quiz.answer: Integrity
quiz.explanation: The configuration has been altered, so the integrity of the system state has been compromised.

summary: Security goals describe desired outcomes, while controls implement those outcomes.
Trust boundaries should be explicit enough to support review and testing.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0

lessons.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Exploitation, and Risk
lessons.description: Build precise terminology for host and workload security analysis.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a threat from a vulnerability and an exploit.
Explain how exposure, likelihood, and impact affect risk.
Write a host-security risk statement with a clear asset and consequence.

notes.text: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is a potential cause of harm; an exploit is a method that takes advantage of a weakness. Risk is contextual because the same weakness can matter differently depending on exposure, asset criticality, compensating controls, and operational constraints.

items: Exposure asks whether the weakness is reachable or otherwise usable.
Impact describes what could happen if the weakness is abused.
Controls can reduce probability, impact, or both.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes a vulnerability from an exploit?
options: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method or action that takes advantage of it.
An exploit is always a patch.
A vulnerability is a business process.
quiz.answer: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method or action that takes advantage of it.
quiz.explanation: The terms refer to different stages of risk: weakness versus exploitation method.

summary: Use precise language in findings and change reviews.
Risk decisions should record context and assumptions.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls
NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security

tasks.title: Write a Host Risk Statement
tasks.description: Create three concise security risk statements for a fictional Linux server.
tasks.problemStatement: For each case, name the asset, threat, weakness, impact, likelihood context, and one control.
objectives: Separate threat from vulnerability.
State the business or operational consequence.
Choose a control that addresses the identified path.
requirements: No special tooling is required; use a text editor.
tasks.hint: Start with the protected asset, then describe the attack or failure path.
tasks.solutionCode: Example: "Internet-facing application server has unnecessary administrative service exposure; an external attacker could target the service and gain unauthorized execution, so management access should be restricted to a dedicated admin network and monitored."
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution is intentionally qualitative because the purpose is to practice disciplined risk statements rather than inventing a numerical model.

modules.title: Secure Configuration and Hardening
modules.description: Turn vendor guidance, security baselines, and checklists into measurable host-hardening controls.

lessons.title: Security Baselines and Configuration Checklists
lessons.description: Learn how baseline configurations reduce attack surface and make drift measurable.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of a security baseline.
Use authoritative vendor or industry checklists rather than inventing arbitrary settings.
Design a baseline that includes ownership, exceptions, and verification.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 5 defines security configuration checklists as instructions or technical content used to configure a product to a target risk posture, verify configuration, detect unauthorized changes, or provide evidence of security posture.

items: A baseline is a target state, not a guarantee of security.
Role-specific baselines are better than one universal configuration.
Exceptions should have owners, rationale, and review dates.

quiz.question: What is a core purpose of a security configuration checklist?
options: Define and verify a target configuration for a product and environment
quiz.answer: Define and verify a target configuration for a product and environment
quiz.explanation: Checklists provide repeatable secure-configuration guidance and verification.

summary: Baselines make secure configuration measurable.
NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 5 is the current NIST checklist guidance identified for this course.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 5: National Checklist Program
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Attack Surface Reduction
lessons.description: Reduce exposed functionality without breaking required service behavior.
learningObjectives: Identify unnecessary services, software, protocols, and management paths.
Explain why reducing attack surface should be role-specific.
Design a safe remove-or-disable change process.

items: Every enabled service creates some additional code, permissions, configuration, and monitoring requirements.
Disable unused components rather than relying on obscurity.
Validate dependencies before removing a service.

notes.text:
Linux inventory examples:
ss -lntup
systemctl --type=service --state=running
rpm -qa | head

practicals.title: Inventory and Reduce Listening Services
practicals.description: In a disposable Linux VM, inventory listening services and document one safe attack-surface reduction change.
steps: Run ss -lntup and record the listening sockets.
Use systemctl to identify the owning service where possible.
Select one service that is not required for the lab role.
Stop it in the lab, verify the listener disappears, and record the before/after state.
Document how you would handle rollback in a production change.
practicals.solution: Use ss -lntup to establish the baseline. For a nonessential test service, use systemctl stop <service> in the disposable VM, then re-run ss -lntup. The exact service name depends on the VM; do not stop a required management service.
practicals.output: A before/after service table showing the removed listener and a documented rollback path.

quiz.question: Why is attack-surface reduction valuable?
options: It removes unnecessary exposed functionality and can reduce reachable weaknesses
quiz.answer: It removes unnecessary exposed functionality and can reduce reachable weaknesses
quiz.explanation: Removing unnecessary exposure reduces the number of paths that need to be defended.

summary: Hardening must preserve required business function.
Exposure reduction complements patching and monitoring.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security
Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 Security Hardening

lessons.title: Configuration Drift and Continuous Assurance
lessons.description: Detect when systems move away from the approved security state.
learningObjectives: Define configuration drift.
Choose evidence for detecting high-impact changes.
Explain why recurring verification is needed.

notes.text: Configuration management establishes and maintains system integrity by controlling how configurations are initialized, changed, and monitored. Drift occurs when actual state diverges from approved state.

A simple desired-state record might contain:
ssh_password_authentication = false
firewall_default_policy = deny
audit_logging = enabled
Do not blindly auto-remediate every drift event; some changes are legitimate emergency or application changes.

quiz.question: What does configuration drift mean?
options: Actual configuration differs from the approved or intended configuration
The operating system has no users
quiz.answer: Actual configuration differs from the approved or intended configuration
quiz.explanation: Drift is divergence between the desired state and current state.

summary: Security baselines become useful when they can be assessed repeatedly.
Change control and drift detection are complementary.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 5: National Checklist Program
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls

tasks.title: Create a Secure Server Baseline
tasks.description: Build a concise baseline for a Linux application server.
tasks.problemStatement: Specify baseline requirements for accounts, SSH, firewalling, logging, patching, file permissions, and service exposure, with verification evidence for each.
objectives: Write measurable controls.
Distinguish required services from unnecessary services.
Include an exception and review process.
requirements: A baseline entry should say what must be true and how you would verify it.
hint: Python 3.11+ or a spreadsheet is sufficient; no third-party packages are required.
tasks.solutionCode:
Baseline excerpt:
- SSH password authentication: disabled where approved key-based access exists
- Management port: reachable only from management network
- Audit logging: enabled and retained centrally
- Unused network services: disabled
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution demonstrates measurable desired states instead of vague recommendations.

modules.title: Identity, Privilege, and Access Control
modules.description: Secure local accounts, service identities, privileges, and administrative access paths.

lessons.title: Local Accounts, Groups, and Lifecycle
lessons.description: Understand account provisioning, review, and deprovisioning on secured hosts.
learningObjectives: Explain why account lifecycle is a security control.
Inspect users and group membership safely.
Identify stale or over-privileged accounts for review.

notes.text:
Linux inspection:
getent passwd
getent group
lastlog

items: Use named service identities where practical.
Remove or disable stale access according to policy.
Review group membership as an effective privilege boundary.

quiz.question: Why is stale account access dangerous?
options: They can preserve unnecessary access after the original business need ends
quiz.answer: They can preserve unnecessary access after the original business need ends
quiz.explanation: Unused identities are unnecessary attack and misuse paths.

summary: Identity lifecycle is broader than authentication.
Access reviews should consider groups and service accounts.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Least Privilege and Linux Capabilities
lessons.description: Move beyond an all-or-nothing root model by understanding Linux capabilities.
learningObjectives: Explain least privilege for human and service accounts.
Describe Linux capabilities as distinct units of privilege.
Identify why a process may need one privileged operation without needing full root authority.

notes.text: Linux capabilities divide traditional superuser privileges into distinct units that can be independently enabled or disabled for processes. This can support more granular privilege design.

Inspect file capabilities where the platform supports them:
getcap /path/to/program
Capabilities can be highly security-sensitive. Grant only the exact capability needed and review why it is required.

quiz.question: What is a Linux capability?
options: A distinct unit of privilege that can be independently controlled
quiz.answer: A distinct unit of privilege that can be independently controlled
quiz.explanation: Linux capabilities split traditional superuser privileges into distinct permission units.

summary: Least privilege reduces the impact of compromise.
Capabilities are a mechanism, not a reason to avoid ordinary access controls.

resources.title: Linux capabilities(7)

lessons.title: Administrative Access and Secure Remote Management
lessons.description: Secure administrative sessions and minimize remote-management exposure.
learningObjectives: Explain why administrative interfaces require strong controls.
Describe key-based SSH access and restrictive daemon configuration.
Plan a management-network-only access path.

notes.text:
Example sshd_config intent:
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowGroups sysadmin
The exact permitted directives depend on the installed OpenSSH version and distribution. Changes should be validated with the daemon configuration checker before restart where available.
Do not disable an administrative access path blindly. Ensure an alternate, tested administrative channel exists first.

practicals.title: Validate SSH Configuration Before Change
practicals.description: Practice inspecting an SSH daemon configuration and validating it before any restart.
steps: Back up the lab sshd_config file.
Review PasswordAuthentication, PermitRootLogin, and AllowGroups settings.
Edit only in the disposable VM if a change is required.
Run the platform-supported configuration test before restart.
Record the configuration evidence and rollback command/file.
practicals.solution: For OpenSSH, review /etc/ssh/sshd_config and validate with sshd -t before restarting. The exact command path may vary by distribution. Never disable an administrative path without a tested alternate access channel.
practicals.output: A configuration-review record with validated syntax and a rollback plan.

quiz.question: Which control most directly reduces remote SSH exposure?
options: Restricting SSH to approved management paths and identities
quiz.answer: Restricting SSH to approved management paths and identities
quiz.explanation: Limiting both network source and identity scope reduces unnecessary administrative exposure.

summary: Remote administration is a high-value trust boundary.
Treat configuration changes as controlled changes with rollback options.

resources.title: OpenBSD sshd_config(5)
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

tasks.title: Design a Privileged Access Model
tasks.description: Create a least-privilege access model for a Linux web server.
tasks.problemStatement: Define human administrator roles, service identities, group membership, SSH policy, and one exception process.
objectives: Separate human and service identities.
Avoid shared administrator accounts.
Restrict remote management to authorized paths.
requirements: Ask which operations truly require elevated rights rather than which users should be "root".
hint: Use a text editor; no special tools required.
tasks.solutionCode: A defensible model might use an unprivileged admin account with controlled elevation, a separate deployment identity, and a service account with no interactive shell when not needed.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The design minimizes standing privilege and keeps service identity separate from human administration.

modules.title: Filesystem, Process, and Isolation Security
modules.description: Protect data and execution boundaries through permissions, MAC, sandboxing, and isolation controls.

lessons.title: Unix File Permissions and ACLs
lessons.description: Use discretionary access controls correctly and recognize their limits.
learningObjectives: Interpret owner/group/other permission bits.
Explain ACLs as more granular access rules.
Identify risky writable paths and sensitive files.

notes.text:
Example:
-rw-r----- 1 app app 1200 config.ini

items: Owner: read/write.
Group: read.
Others: no access.
Effective access can also depend on ACLs and group membership.

quiz.question: What is a key risk of unnecessary world-writable configuration files?
options: Unintended users may alter security-sensitive configuration
quiz.answer: Unintended users may alter security-sensitive configuration
quiz.explanation: Broad write permissions can allow tampering with configuration or program inputs.

summary: Use the narrowest write access compatible with operation.
Check effective access, not only the visible mode bits.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Mandatory Access Control with SELinux
lessons.description: Understand MAC policy as a second layer beyond traditional file permissions.
learningObjectives: Differentiate DAC and MAC.
Explain enforcing and permissive SELinux modes.
Use labels and policy concepts to reason about denied access.

notes.text: SELinux is a mandatory access-control system that can constrain interactions based on security policy even when traditional Unix permissions would allow an action. Red Hat documents SELinux as an important part of host hardening.

Useful status checks on systems using SELinux:
getenforce
sestatus
Changing SELinux to permissive or disabling it may hide policy failures rather than solving them; investigate the policy decision and required label or rule.

practicals.title: Observe SELinux Enforcement
practicals.description: On a Red Hat-family lab VM where SELinux is available, compare policy behavior with normal Unix permissions.
steps: Run getenforce and record the mode.
Inspect the security context of a service-related file with ls -Z.
Review an existing denial or controlled lab condition rather than disabling SELinux.
Explain which DAC permission would allow the operation and which MAC policy could still deny it.
Restore the lab to its original state.
practicals.solution: The student records the SELinux mode and contexts, then explains the layered decision: Unix DAC may permit an operation while SELinux policy still restricts it. The exercise does not require changing enforcement state.
practicals.output: A short evidence note demonstrating the difference between DAC and MAC.

quiz.question: How does SELinux complement traditional Unix permissions?
options: It can enforce additional policy constraints on processes and resources beyond DAC rules
quiz.answer: It can enforce additional policy constraints on processes and resources beyond DAC rules
quiz.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory policy enforcement in addition to traditional discretionary permissions.

summary: Mandatory controls are useful when application compromise must not automatically grant broad resource access.
Use vendor policy guidance rather than ad hoc policy rules.

resources.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 Security Hardening

lessons.title: Process Sandboxing and Service Isolation
lessons.description: Reduce the impact of compromised or misbehaving services.
learningObjectives: Explain process isolation as a defense-in-depth control.
Identify useful sandboxing dimensions such as filesystem, network, device, and privilege restrictions.
Design isolation without hiding required dependencies.

items: A service can be restricted from writing sensitive paths even if its account has some local permissions.
Isolation controls can reduce access to devices, kernel interfaces, or network destinations.
Modern Linux service managers can combine several sandboxing primitives; exact directives are platform/version dependent.

notes.text:
Conceptual service policy:
Protect sensitive filesystems
Restrict device access
Drop unnecessary privileges
Limit network destinations

quiz.question: What is the main security benefit of sandboxing a service?
options: It guarantees the service is bug-free
It limits the resources and authority available to the service if it is compromised
It removes the need for authentication
quiz.answer: It limits the resources and authority available to the service if it is compromised
quiz.explanation: Isolation reduces post-compromise reach and blast radius.

summary: Isolation should be layered with least privilege and secure configuration.
Measure the service dependencies before tightening a sandbox.

resources.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 Security Hardening
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls

tasks.title: Harden a Service Identity and Filesystem
tasks.description: Design access controls for a service that reads application data and writes temporary files.
tasks.problemStatement: Specify the account, directories, permissions, ACL or MAC considerations, and isolation boundaries needed to prevent modification of unrelated system files.
objectives: Minimize writable locations.
Separate application data from system configuration.
Explain one defense against path traversal or unexpected file replacement.
requirements: Map every required read/write path before granting permissions.
hint: A diagram is optional; a table plus configuration examples is sufficient.
tasks.solutionCode: A strong design gives the service a dedicated identity, read-only access to required application assets, a narrow writable directory for temporary data, and additional isolation to prevent access to unrelated system paths.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution emphasizes containment: a compromised service should have as little filesystem authority as its function requires.

modules.title: Patching, Software Integrity, and Configuration Assurance
modules.description: Maintain secure system state through updates, software provenance, integrity checks, and compliance verification.

lessons.title: Patch Management and Maintenance Windows
lessons.description: Build a repeatable patching workflow rather than ad hoc updates.
learningObjectives: Describe patch intake, risk assessment, testing, deployment, verification, and rollback.
Distinguish security updates from feature changes.
Document exceptions and deferred patches.

items: Patch management is a lifecycle process.
Critical systems may need maintenance windows and staged deployment.
Compensating controls may reduce exposure when immediate patching is impossible.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-123 describes securing and maintaining servers; patching should be integrated with asset ownership, configuration management, and operational change processes.

quiz.question: Why should patch deployment include verification?
options: To confirm the intended security condition actually changed and services still function
quiz.answer: To confirm the intended security condition actually changed and services still function
quiz.explanation: Deployment without verification can leave the vulnerability open or create operational failure.

summary: Patching is both a security and change-management process.
Deferred fixes should remain visible and owned.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Package Provenance and Software Integrity
lessons.description: Protect the trust chain for installed software and updates.
learningObjectives: Explain package provenance and repository trust.
Describe integrity checking and signed package metadata at a high level.
Identify suspicious manual installation paths.

notes.text: Software integrity depends on knowing where software came from and whether the expected artifact was altered. Enterprise environments should prefer managed repositories, verified signatures, controlled build sources, and change records.

items: Do not copy binaries from untrusted sources as a routine practice.
Verify package signatures or repository metadata according to the platform.
Track versions to support vulnerability response.

quiz.question: Why is provenance important for system software?
options: It helps establish source and expected integrity of components
quiz.answer: It helps establish source and expected integrity of components
quiz.explanation: Provenance supports trust, reproducibility, and incident investigation.

summary: Software supply-chain trust begins with source and integrity.
Security teams should know how deployed components entered the system.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Compliance Scanning and Control Assessment
lessons.description: Use evidence-based assessments to measure whether controls are implemented as intended.
learningObjectives: Differentiate configuration scanning from control assessment.
Collect evidence without making unsupported claims.
Write a finding that states condition, evidence, risk, and recommendation.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-53A provides assessment procedures for security and privacy controls. A useful assessment distinguishes the control requirement from the evidence that shows implementation and from the assessor conclusion.

Finding structure:
Condition -> Evidence -> Risk -> Recommendation
Example evidence: configuration file, command output, policy record, log sample

practicals.title: Write a Control Assessment Finding
practicals.description: Turn a small set of host evidence into an auditable security finding.
steps: Collect evidence for three controls from a lab VM.
For each control, state the expected condition.
Record the observed evidence exactly enough for another reviewer to reproduce it.
Classify the control as pass, fail, or insufficient evidence.
Write one measurable remediation and one verification step.
practicals.solution: A good solution preserves raw evidence and clearly separates the observed condition from interpretation. For insufficient evidence, the correct result is not "secure" or "failed"; it is a documented evidence gap requiring follow-up.
practicals.output: Three completed findings containing criterion, evidence, conclusion, remediation, and verification.

quiz.question: What is an important difference between a scan result and an assessment conclusion?
options: A scan produces evidence or indications; an assessment interprets evidence against defined criteria
quiz.answer: A scan produces evidence or indications; an assessment interprets evidence against defined criteria
quiz.explanation: Assessment requires defined criteria and interpretation of evidence.

summary: Avoid overstating what a scanner proves.
Evidence should be attributable and reproducible.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5: Assessing Security and Privacy Controls
NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 5: National Checklist Program

tasks.title: Create an Evidence-Based Hardening Finding
tasks.description: Turn raw configuration evidence into a professional system-security finding.
tasks.problemStatement: Given three configuration observations, produce findings containing condition, evidence, risk, recommendation, and verification steps.
objectives: Keep evidence separate from inference.
State technical and business impact clearly.
Make recommendations testable.
requirements: Do not call a host "secure" because one setting is correct.
hint: Use a markdown document; no special tooling is required.
tasks.solutionCode: Example: "SSH password authentication remains enabled. Evidence: effective sshd configuration includes PasswordAuthentication yes. Risk: password-based remote access increases credential-attack exposure. Recommendation: move approved users to key-based authentication and validate access before disabling password authentication."
tasks.solutionExplanation: The structure forces claims to remain traceable to evidence and makes remediation verifiable.

modules.title: Endpoint Protection and Host Telemetry
modules.description: Secure Windows and Linux endpoints using built-in protections, logging, integrity monitoring, and secure defaults.

lessons.title: Windows Security Architecture and Baselines
lessons.description: Understand Windows security features and how Microsoft baselines provide a starting point.
learningObjectives: Identify major Windows security layers such as UAC, Defender, firewalling, BitLocker, and security baselines.
Explain why enterprise baselines should be adapted and tested.
Distinguish baseline settings from product licensing and environment-specific requirements.

notes.text: Microsoft publishes security baselines for supported Windows versions. The baseline guidance is intended to provide broadly tested configuration recommendations rather than asking every organization to invent settings from scratch.

items: Windows security includes OS, identity, application, data, and hardware protections.
Baselines should be applied through managed configuration mechanisms where practical.
Validate changes against business applications before broad rollout.

quiz.question: Why use an established Windows security baseline?
options: It guarantees every threat is blocked
It provides a broadly tested starting configuration with documented security rationale
quiz.answer: It provides a broadly tested starting configuration with documented security rationale
quiz.explanation: Established baselines reduce arbitrary configuration choices and provide repeatable guidance.

summary: Baseline guidance is a starting point, not the whole security program.
Use the version appropriate to the supported Windows release.

resources.title: Microsoft Security Baselines
Windows Security Documentation

lessons.title: Linux Host Security and Hardening Layers
lessons.description: Integrate Linux accounts, permissions, services, MAC, logging, and updates.
learningObjectives: Assemble a layered Linux hardening strategy.
Identify which controls operate at account, process, filesystem, network, and kernel layers.
Explain why hardening must be role-specific.

items: Layered controls include identity, permissions, service minimization, mandatory access control, firewalling, logging, updates, and secure remote administration.
Do not apply a hardening guide without understanding application dependencies.

notes.text:
Example review commands:
id
ss -lntup
getenforce
stat /path/to/sensitive/file
journalctl -b -p warning

quiz.question: Which statement best describes layered Linux hardening?
options: Combine controls at multiple system layers so one failure does not expose the entire host
quiz.answer: Combine controls at multiple system layers so one failure does not expose the entire host
quiz.explanation: Defense in depth aims to reduce single-control failure impact.

summary: Host hardening works when controls reinforce each other.
Role-specific configuration is safer than indiscriminate lockdown.

resources.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 Security Hardening
NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security

lessons.title: Endpoint Logging and Auditability
lessons.description: Ensure important host actions leave useful, protected evidence.
learningObjectives: Identify valuable endpoint telemetry sources.
Explain why time synchronization and log protection matter.
Design a minimum audit-log set for a server role.

items: Useful sources may include authentication, privilege changes, service starts, configuration changes, process activity, and security-product alerts.
Centralization improves correlation and resilience against local log loss.
Logs can contain sensitive information and need access controls and retention policy.

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of centralized endpoint logs?
options: They preserve and correlate events beyond the individual host
They remove the need for authentication
quiz.answer: They preserve and correlate events beyond the individual host
quiz.explanation: Centralized logs improve investigation and correlation across systems.

summary: Logging is an evidence capability as well as a detection capability.
Protect the logs themselves from unauthorized modification.

resources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.2.0: Security and Privacy Controls

tasks.title: Endpoint Baseline Review
tasks.description: Assess a fictional Windows or Linux workstation against a defined security baseline.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a gap table with control, expected state, observed evidence, risk, owner, and remediation priority.
objectives: Use vendor or standards-based control language.
Separate missing evidence from failed controls.
Prioritize based on likely risk reduction.
requirements: A missing screenshot or command result is evidence insufficiency, not automatically a failed control.
hint: Use a text editor or spreadsheet.
tasks.solutionCode: The expected output is an auditable table rather than a narrative-only review.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task develops repeatable endpoint-assurance practice and careful evidence handling.

modules.title: Service Security and Secure System Operations
modules.description: Secure services through safe defaults, configuration validation, resource boundaries, and maintenance discipline.

lessons.title: Secure Service Configuration
lessons.description: Review service listeners, authentication settings, privileges, and security-sensitive defaults.
learningObjectives: Create a service-security review checklist.
Identify insecure defaults and unnecessary listeners.
Explain how configuration errors can bypass otherwise strong host controls.

notes.text:
Review pattern:
1. Identify exposed interfaces.
2. Confirm required authentication.
3. Confirm least privilege.
4. Verify secure logging.
5. Validate configuration syntax.
6. Restart through approved change procedure.
Never change a production daemon configuration without an alternate administrative path, backup/rollback plan, and syntax validation.

quiz.question: Why are service defaults security-sensitive?
options: A default can enable unnecessary access, weak authentication, or broader exposure than intended
quiz.answer: A default can enable unnecessary access, weak authentication, or broader exposure than intended
quiz.explanation: Initial configurations often determine exposure until deliberately changed.

summary: Service security is configuration plus operational discipline.
Read version-specific vendor documentation before applying settings.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-123: Guide to General Server Security
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1

lessons.title: Resource Limits and Availability Security
lessons.description: Use limits to reduce denial-of-service impact and runaway process behavior.
learningObjectives: Explain resource exhaustion as a security problem.
Identify CPU, memory, file, process, and connection limits that may matter for a service.
Balance protective limits with service requirements.

notes.text: Availability security includes protecting systems from resource exhaustion. Limits can reduce blast radius when a process behaves unexpectedly, but limits that are too low can cause self-inflicted outages.

Design question:
What is the normal resource envelope?
What limit contains abnormal behavior without breaking legitimate load?

quiz.question: Why should resource limits be tested before enforcement?
options: Poorly chosen limits can create outages or break legitimate workloads

lessons.title: File Integrity and Unauthorized Change Detection
lessons.description: Detect meaningful changes to system files and configuration.
learningObjectives: Explain file-integrity monitoring.

notes.text: File-integrity monitoring compares current state with known-good state or expected metadata. It is most useful when focused on security-sensitive files and correlated with change management.

Example integrity workflow:
1. Record baseline hash.
2. Detect changed file.
3. Compare against approved change.
4. Collect surrounding logs.
5. Escalate if unexplained.

summary: Integrity monitoring detects change, not intent.

lessons.title: Incident Containment and Recovery on Hosts
lessons.description: Apply host containment, eradication, and recovery principles safely.
learningObjectives: Differentiate containment, eradication, and recovery.
Choose reversible containment actions when practical.
Verify restored security state before returning systems to service.

items: Containment limits ongoing harm. Eradication removes the cause or foothold. Recovery restores trustworthy service and monitoring.
Rebuild from a trusted image may be safer than attempting to clean an extensively compromised host, depending on evidence and operational constraints.

notes.text: Do not destroy evidence or disconnect critical systems without considering legal, operational, and investigative requirements.

quiz.explanation: Recovery returns the service to a trustworthy operational condition.

summary: Containment, eradication, and recovery are related but distinct.
Verification should include security controls, not only application uptime.

lessons.title: Project Architecture and Security Requirements
lessons.description: Plan a read-only local system-security audit tool around measurable controls and safe evidence collection.
learningObjectives: Define the capstone architecture and control set.

notes.text: The capstone is deliberately read-only. It checks a compact baseline covering root-shell state, world-writable files directly under /etc, SSH configuration, and package-manager presence. items: The project is an assessment tool, not an auto-remediation engine.

code.README.md:
# System Security Baseline Auditor

A local-only training utility that audits a Linux host against a small, explicitly defined security baseline. It reports pass/fail/unknown states and never changes the system.

The tool intentionally uses only Python's standard library so it can be reviewed and tested without third-party dependencies.
code.test_audit_baseline.py:
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def test_cli_outputs_valid_json():
    result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT / "audit_baseline.py")], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    report = json.loads(result.stdout)
    assert report["tool_scope"] == "local-only, read-only training audit"
    assert report["finding_count"] == 4
    assert all(set(item) == {"control", "status", "evidence", "recommendation"} for item in report["findings"])

def test_json_output_file(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "report.json"
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT / "audit_baseline.py"), "--json", str(out)], check=True)
    report = json.loads(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    assert len(report["findings"]) == 4

project.explanation: The project implements a simple assessment pipeline: local evidence collection -> control-specific evaluation -> structured finding -> report. It deliberately uses three result states (pass, review, unknown) to avoid overstating evidence. The code is read-only and standard-library-only, which makes it easy to review and test. The project demonstrates how configuration management, least privilege, secure remote administration, filesystem security, and assessment methodology combine into an auditable system-security workflow.
